notes.meaning: Mordecai learned about the royal order to destroy his people. He tore his clothes, wore rough sackcloth, put ashes on his head, and cried loudly in the streets. He was not afraid to show his deep grief openly and stand with his fellow Jews.

Mordecai walked as far as the entrance to the palace, but Persian law stopped him from going inside. The king did not allow anyone dressed in mourning clothes to enter his gate. The rulers wanted court life to seem carefree, foolishly trying to shut out signs of trouble while causing misery for others.

In every corner of the empire where the royal decree arrived, the Jews were filled with terror and grief. They wept, wailed, and refused to eat, and many lay on the ground in sackcloth and ashes. Even though prayer is not named directly, fasting was their traditional way of humbling themselves before God to seek His help.

Esther’s attendants came and told her that Mordecai was sitting outside in mourning clothes, which caused her great sorrow. She sent new clothes for him to wear so he could look presentable and enter the palace to explain his trouble. Mordecai refused the clothes because his grief over his people was too heavy to cover up.

Esther called Hathach, a trusted palace official appointed to serve her, and sent him to find out why Mordecai was mourning. Hathach went out to the open square just outside the palace gate to speak with him. Because royal Persian women lived in strict privacy, Esther had to rely on messengers to speak with the outside world.

Mordecai explained everything that had happened between himself and Haman. He also revealed the exact amount of silver Haman had offered to pay into the royal treasury to secure permission to wipe out the Jews. This showed Esther how serious the threat was and how deeply Haman was driven by hatred and greed.

Mordecai gave Hathach a written copy of the royal decree that had been announced in Susa so Esther could read it herself. He urged her to go directly before the king to beg for his favor. Mordecai charged her to plead for the lives of her people before it was too late.

Hathach returned to the palace and reported Mordecai’s words and the horrifying news to Esther. Esther then sent Hathach back to Mordecai with her reply, explaining the great danger of what he was asking her to do.

Esther pointed out a well-known law that carried the death penalty for anyone entering the king's inner court without being summoned. The only exception was if the king held out his golden scepter to spare the person's life. Esther had not been invited to see the king for thirty days, which made her worry that she had fallen out of his favor.

Hathach carried Esther’s answer to Mordecai, and Mordecai sent back a sharp warning. He told her not to think that living inside the royal palace would shield her from the coming massacre. Because she was a Jew, she was under the same death sentence as the rest of her people.

Mordecai expressed bold faith that if Esther stayed silent, God would still deliver the Jews through another way. But he warned that she and her father's household would be destroyed for holding back. He suggested that God's hidden purpose in making her queen was to save her people at this very moment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read the sentence as a doubtful question, arguing that Mordecai did not expect help from anywhere else and saw Esther as the only possible hope.

notes.meaning: Esther answered by asking Mordecai to gather all the Jews in Susa for a three-day fast, while she and her female attendants did the same. After seeking help through fasting, she resolved to go before the king even though it broke the royal law. She placed her life completely in God's hands, saying that if she died doing her duty, she accepted it.
Mordecai left his post outside the palace gate and carried out everything Esther had requested. He brought the Jewish community together to observe the solemn fast for her mission.
